current_episode.title: The Insane Productivity of Andrew Ross Sorkin

guest.bio_context: Andrew Ross Sorkin joined the New York Times at age 18 in 1995 after creating Sports Page Magazine in high school in Scarsdale, New York. He founded DealBook in 2001 as an email newsletter covering mergers and acquisitions and has grown it to over one million subscribers over 25 years. He is the co-creator of the television series Billions, has authored two major books—Too Big to Fail and 1929—and hosts the annual Dealbook Summit every December.

context.real_quote: I think it's important to understand what their motivation is. pending_qa.q: What was the first advertiser for DealBook when it launched?
pending_qa.r: The original advertiser for DealBook was Brooks Brothers. Sorkin notes that while Brooks Brothers is still in business today, they have gone in and out of business a couple of times since then.

pending_qa.q: How does a media professional manage multiple demanding roles simultaneously across television, newsletters, and books?
pending_qa.r: Andrew Ross Sorkin's day typically begins around 4:30 in the morning, when he wakes up and checks email and messages under the covers. He spends about an hour before Squawk Box starts (which runs from 6 a.m. to 9 a.m. Eastern) making tweaks to the DealBook newsletter. The newsletter team, which has grown significantly, includes colleagues like Michael Dillamer who has been with him for about 20 years, and Bernard Warner working overnight from Italy. Sorkin notes that all these projects inform each other in interesting ways, allowing him to have the best of both worlds.

pending_qa.q: How should journalists approach sources who have mixed or ulterior motives for sharing information?
pending_qa.r: Sorkin believes every source has some motivation for talking, and it is typically self-interested. Rather than worrying about their ultimate incentives, he focuses on confirming information from two, three, or four different sources or obtaining documentation. He notes that some of the best sources have completely terrible and ulterior motives—people wanting to screw someone else over, board members trying to stop or advance deals, or bankers who have lost business to competitors and want to leak information.

pending_qa.q: What is the role of junior employees and 'jilted' insiders in uncovering major business stories?
pending_qa.r: Great stories often start at very junior levels, not just with senior people. Sorkin identifies what he calls the 'jilted somebody'—someone who lost an auction, was passed over for business by a competitor, or spent years cultivating a client relationship only to see Goldman Sachs win the account instead. These individuals have no remaining stake in the game except the ability to upset the situation, making them more inclined to leak information or provide insights to reporters.

pending_qa.q: What was the initial market size expectation for DealBook compared to its actual growth?
pending_qa.r: When launching DealBook during the dot-com bust, the New York Times thought the total addressable market was 30,000 free subscribers. Today, DealBook has grown to over one million subscribers, far exceeding initial projections.

pending_qa.q: How did Andrew Ross Sorkin's first assignment at the New York Times happen?
pending_qa.r: In 1995, Sorkin was coming to the New York Times office with a visitor pass, wearing a suit and tie, and performing clerical tasks like Xeroxing and stapling. An editor who had no idea how old he was overheard him talking about the Internet and assigned him a story to write. His first published piece was about the noise that modems make, explaining to readers that the noise was the two modems 'talking to each other' over a phone line.

pending_qa.q: What was Andrew Ross Sorkin's business venture before joining the New York Times full-time?
pending_qa.r: At age 15, Sorkin created Sports Page Magazine at Scarsdale High School, which published sports journalism written by high school students and targeted young male readers through advertising. The magazines were distributed across the country inside high schools. He spent about a year successfully selling ads at $900 to $1,200 per full-page ad, but the venture ultimately failed by age 18 due to operational mistakes—including expensive Federal Express shipping for mailings and miscalculating printing costs with the same printer that worked with Wired magazine.
